newsitem.title: USA: Wheelchair-bound Clinton heads for Helsinki summit.
newsitem.headline: Wheelchair-bound Clinton heads for Helsinki summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday headed for Finland and his summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, upbeat despite physical discomfort from his damaged knee and fiery rhetoric from Moscow on NATO expansion.

White House officials said Clinton was looking forward to his first personal encounter with Yeltsin since an April meeting last year, although his trip had been complicated and shortened by surgery to reattach a torn tendon.

The president, who injured his knee last week when he stumbled down stairs at the Florida home of Australian golfer Greg Norman, essentially has been confined to a wheelchair since he was released from hospital last Sunday.
The accident forced a day's delay in the start of the U.S.-Russian summit and meant adding extra medical staff, including an orthopedist and a physical therapist, to Clinton's travelling party.
Ironically, Helsinki replaced Washington as the summit site in order to make the trip less arduous for Yeltsin, who had heart bypass surgery late last year and then struggled with double pneumonia.
As Clinton prepared to leave on Wednesday, a Kremlin spokesman raised the rhetoric over NATO expansion another notch, predicting it would be the West's biggest blunder since the end of the Cold War.

The anti-NATO tirade from Moscow, and the equally insistent tone from Washington that enlargement of the alliance to former Soviet bloc countries was a as good as done, appeared to set a hostile tone for the Clinton-Yeltsin meetings on Thursday and Friday.

But U.S. officials stressed that dramatic breakthroughs had never been expected from this summit. Instead, they hoped for progress in smoothing over the divisive issue as well as some movement toward a charter spelling out NATO-Russia ties.
For his part, Clinton focused on Yeltsin's latest Kremlin changes, declaring himself encouraged by the Russian leader's "new economic theme."
Yeltsin in recent days has shaken up his Cabinet in a move intended to re-establish authority after his long illness and to bring market-oriented economic reformers into senior posts.
"Now the challenge is to create a climate that actually attracts more investment and promotes more trade so that Russia will have real ecomnomic growth," Clinton said.
The president acknowledged that enlarging NATO was a top priority and stressed that he wanted to build a "robust" partnership between the alliance and Russia.
But Clinton gave equal weight to arms control issues and economic progress.

"We will focus on three important areas. First, on moving forward with our work to build a Europe that is undivided, democratic and at peace for the first time in the history of the continent," he said. "Second, on continuing to reduce the danger of weapons of mass destruction and third, on expanding the economic partnership that is good for Americans and Russians alike."
Clinton will return to Washington at the weekend. He cancelled plans to visit Denmark after the summit because of his knee injury.
